As $\abs{Q-a}^{-1/2}\le1$ when $\abs{Q-a}>1$, it follows that $\E\abs{Q-a}^{-1/2}<77$.

excerpt: The number five is used only in the case without pivots, through Proposition~\ref{prop:signs} with $m=3$; the diagonal pivot uses four large eigenvalues of $A$ and the pair cases use three. Four eigenvalues without pivots need not give a third large singular value in any off-diagonal block. Let $N>256$, let $w\in\R^N$ have all entries equal to $N^{-1/2}$, and let $A$ be the direct sum of two copies of the $(N+1)\times(N+1)$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&w^T\\w&0\end{pmatrix}$. Its nonzero eigenvalues are $1,1,-1,-1$, its diagonal vanishes and every principal $2\times2$ minor has modulus at most $1/N<\zeta$, so $A$ has no pivot. For every partition $[n]=I\sqcup J$ the part of each copy in $A_{I,J}$ lies in a single row or a single column, namely that of the centre of the copy, so $A_{I,J}$ has rank at most two and $E_3(A_{I,J})=0$.
derivation: Each weighted-star block has eigenvalues ±1 and zeros because ||w||=1; two copies give four nonzero eigenvalues. Diagonal is zero, every 2x2 principal minor has modulus 0 or 1/N<zeta, and each copy contributes crossing rank<=1 for any partition, so total crossing rank<=2 and E3=0. This is a limitation of the order-three-crossing method, not a counterexample to a four-eigenvalue density theorem.
